plan: Eight new SAT R&W items aimed at upper difficulty (overstate WIC, ferry literary function, desert-seed germination inference, equal-gain percent data, nonessential clause closing comma, long-subject agreement, evidently transition, axolotl new-audience synthesis) plus S049-06 and S049-10 resubmitted as revision 2 (counts in every distractor; key reworded to the notes). S049-07 stays rejected as a near-duplicate of CLD-SAT-RW-000106. Difficulty provisional. Solver note: S050-04 and S050-09 share a percent-versus-count structure (opposite directions); kept, noted for set assembly.

passages.title: Early results
passages.text: Although the new treatment's early results were promising, the researchers were careful not to ______ them, noting that the trial had included only forty patients and had lasted just six weeks.

passages.title: The ferry
passages.text: The old ferry had crossed the river twice a day for sixty years. Most people in town no longer noticed its horn. When the county announced that a new bridge would replace it, people who had not ridden the ferry in decades wrote letters to the newspaper demanding that it be saved.

passages.title: Desert seeds
passages.text: The seeds of a certain desert plant contain a chemical that prevents them from germinating. Heavy rainfall washes the chemical out of the seed coat, but a light shower does not. In laboratory tests, seeds soaked in water for a few minutes rarely germinated, while seeds soaked for several hours germinated readily. This mechanism likely benefits the plant because ______

passages.title: Two cities
passages.text:
A demographer compared the populations of two cities.
City A: 50,000 residents in 2000; 80,000 residents in 2020.
City B: 120,000 residents in 2000; 150,000 residents in 2020.
The demographer claims that although the two cities gained the same number of residents, city A grew much faster in percentage terms.

passages.title: A popular gallery
passages.text: The museum's newest gallery, which opened in ______ already drawn more visitors than any other exhibit in the building's history.

passages.title: A summer tradition
passages.text: The tradition of building sandcastles on the town's beach each July, which began more than a century ago as a contest for local children, ______ to draw thousands of visitors every summer.

passages.title: An unexplored cave
passages.text: Early accounts described the cave as a single, modest chamber. Later surveys found it to be far larger, with dozens of connected passages stretching for kilometers. ______ the original explorers, working by candlelight, had seen only the entrance hall.

passages.title: Axolotl regrowth
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The axolotl is a salamander native to lakes near Mexico City.
- Unlike most salamanders, it keeps its gills and lives in water as an adult.
- It can regrow lost limbs, including bone and muscle.
- Researchers have found that axolotls regrow limbs more slowly as they age.

passages.title: Rural and urban survey
passages.text: In a state survey, 200 rural residents and 800 urban residents were asked whether they had used a public library in the past month. Of the rural residents, 30 percent said yes; of the urban residents, 20 percent said yes. A reporter claims that more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library, even though a smaller percentage of urban residents had.

passages.title: Two great rivers
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river.
- The Congo River carries the second-largest volume of water.
- Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
- The Amazon is roughly 6,400 kilometers long; the Congo is roughly 4,700 kilometers long.
- Parts of the Congo are more than 200 meters deep.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.explanation: The small, short trial is a reason not to claim too much, so the researchers were careful not to "overstate" the results.

A.rationale: "Although" sets up a contrast with promising results; being careful not to dismiss them would not contrast with their promise.

B.rationale: Replicating results is what careful researchers want; the caution here is about how strongly to describe them.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the researchers might hide the results; they are discussing their limits.

hints: Why does the text mention forty patients and six weeks?

strategy.explanation: Predict "make them sound bigger than they are."

candidates.remember: Limits on a study signal caution about claiming too much.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It suggests that the ferry's horn had grown too faint over the years for people in town to hear.
choices.B: It shows the ferry had become an unnoticed part of town life, making the later outcry surprising.
choices.C: It explains why the county decided that a bridge should replace the old ferry.
choices.D: It indicates that most people in town would not object to replacing the ferry.

candidates.evidence: Most people in town no longer noticed its horn.
candidates.explanation: The second sentence establishes the townspeople's indifference, which sets up the irony that people who ignored the ferry fought to save it.

A.rationale: The townspeople stopped noticing the horn out of habit; nothing suggests it became quieter.

C.rationale: The text gives no reason for the county's decision.

D.rationale: Many people did object, including some who had not ridden the ferry in decades.

hints: How does the second sentence relate to the last one?

strategy.explanation: Compare what people did before and after the announcement.

candidates.remember: A detail early in a literary text often sets up a contrast later.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: it keeps seeds from sprouting after rains too light to support young plants.
choices.B: it allows the seeds to sprout after any amount of rain, however small.
choices.C: it protects the seeds from being eaten by animals living in the desert.
choices.D: it makes the seeds heavy enough that strong winds cannot carry them away.

candidates.evidence: Heavy rainfall washes the chemical out of the seed coat, but a light shower does not.
candidates.explanation: Seeds germinate only after enough rain to wash out the chemical, so they avoid sprouting when there is too little water for seedlings to survive.

B.rationale: The chemical prevents germination after light showers, so the seeds do not sprout after any rain.

C.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns animals eating the seeds.

D.rationale: The text says nothing about the seeds' weight or about wind.

hints: When do the seeds germinate, and why would that help in a desert?

strategy.explanation: Connect the trigger for germination to desert conditions.

candidates.remember: A good inference connects the mechanism to the conditions the organism faces.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the demographer's claim?

choices.A: City A grew from 50,000 to 80,000 residents, an increase of 30,000 people over twenty years.
choices.B: City B had 120,000 residents in 2000 and 150,000 in 2020, more than city A in both years.
choices.C: Each city gained 30,000 residents, but A grew by 60 percent while B grew by 25 percent.
choices.D: By 2020, city B had 70,000 more residents than city A, nearly twice city A's population.

candidates.evidence: grew much faster in percentage terms
candidates.explanation: Both cities gained 30,000 people, but that is 60 percent of 50,000 and only 25 percent of 120,000. Only C gives both parts of the claim.

A.rationale: This gives city A's change only and does not compare the two cities' percentage growth.

B.rationale: City B's larger size does not address percentage growth.

D.rationale: This compares sizes in 2020, not the cities' growth.

hints: What two things does the claim say?

strategy.explanation: Compute each city's gain and percentage growth.

candidates.remember: Equal gains can be very different percentages of different starting sizes.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The nonessential clause "which opened in March" begins with a comma after "gallery," so it must close with a comma before the verb "has."

B.rationale: Without a comma after "March," the clause "which opened in March" is opened by a comma but never closed.

C.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate the subject "gallery" from its verb "has drawn."

D.rationale: A dash cannot close a clause that was opened with a comma; the punctuation must match.

hints: Where does the interrupting clause begin and end?

strategy.explanation: Match the closing punctuation to the opening comma.

candidates.remember: A nonessential clause in mid-sentence needs matching punctuation on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: Strip away the phrases and clause: "The tradition ... continues to draw thousands of visitors." The singular subject takes the singular verb "continues."

A.rationale: The subject is the singular "tradition," not "sandcastles" or "children."

B.rationale: "Continuing" is not a main verb, so the sentence would have no verb for "tradition."

C.rationale: "Have" is plural and does not agree with the singular "tradition."

hints: What is the subject of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Cross out everything between the subject and the verb.

candidates.remember: A verb agrees with its subject, not with the nearest noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: had seen only the entrance hall
candidates.explanation: The final sentence is a conclusion drawn from the mismatch between the early accounts and the later surveys, so "Evidently" fits.

A.rationale: The later surveys did not cause the original explorers to see only the entrance; that happened earlier.

C.rationale: The final sentence does not describe a similar case; it explains the earlier accounts.

D.rationale: Nothing in the final sentence goes against what came before.

hints: Is the last sentence a result, a comparison, a contrast, or a conclusion drawn from evidence?

strategy.explanation: Ask how the writer knows the final sentence is true.

candidates.remember: Use "evidently" for a conclusion inferred from evidence just given.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (presenting a finding to a new audience)
candidates.stem: The student wants to present the research finding to an audience unfamiliar with axolotls. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Researchers have found that axolotls regrow lost limbs, including bone and muscle, more slowly with age.
choices.B: The axolotl, a salamander from lakes near Mexico City, keeps its gills and lives in water as an adult.
choices.C: Axolotls, salamanders from near Mexico City that can regrow lost limbs, regrow them more slowly with age.
choices.D: Unlike most salamanders, axolotls keep their gills as adults and can even regrow their lost limbs.

candidates.evidence: Researchers have found that axolotls regrow limbs more slowly as they age.
candidates.explanation: Only C both introduces the axolotl (a salamander from near Mexico City that regrows limbs) and states the finding.

A.rationale: This presents the finding but never explains what an axolotl is for an unfamiliar audience.

B.rationale: This introduces the animal but omits the research finding.

D.rationale: This describes the animal's traits but leaves out the finding about age.

hints: What does an unfamiliar audience need besides the finding?

strategy.explanation: Check for an introduction and the finding.

candidates.remember: For a new audience, introduce the subject as you present the point.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the survey to support the reporter's claim?

choices.A: 160 urban residents said yes versus 60 rural residents, though 20 percent is below 30 percent.
choices.B: 60 rural residents said yes, which is 30 percent of the 200 rural residents who were surveyed.
choices.C: 160 urban residents said yes, which is 20 percent of the 800 urban residents who were surveyed.
choices.D: Of the 1,000 residents surveyed, 220 said yes, and 800 of the 1,000 lived in urban areas.

candidates.evidence: more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library
candidates.explanation: 20 percent of 800 is 160 and 30 percent of 200 is 60, so more urban residents said yes even though their percentage was lower. Only A gives both parts.

B.rationale: This gives only the rural count and percentage, so it cannot show that more urban residents said yes.

C.rationale: This gives only the urban count and percentage, so it cannot show that more urban than rural residents said yes.

D.rationale: A combined total does not show how the yes answers split between urban and rural residents.

hints: What would you need to compute to compare numbers of people?

strategy.explanation: Convert each percentage to a count.

candidates.remember: A smaller percentage of a larger group can still be a larger number.

revision_history.reason: solvers: key was the only choice with counts; distractors now also give counts, so both parts of the claim must be checked

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two rivers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: At roughly 6,400 kilometers, the Amazon is about 1,700 kilometers longer than the 4,700-kilometer Congo.
choices.B: Parts of the Congo River are more than 200 meters deep, making it unusually deep for a river.
choices.C: The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river anywhere on Earth, including the Congo.
choices.D: The Amazon and Congo both drain large tropical rainforests and rank first and second in water volume.

candidates.evidence: Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
candidates.explanation: Only D describes features the two rivers share: both drain rainforests and both are at the top in volume.

A.rationale: This emphasizes a difference in length, not a similarity.

hints: Which choice mentions both rivers and something they have in common?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: For a similarity goal, the answer must describe both items and what they share.

revision_history.reason: solvers: "more water than any other rivers" loose and "vast" beyond notes; key reworded to the notes ranking
